tool.name: TRI
tool.summary: Computes a Terrain Ruggedness Index (TRI): a per-cell measure of how much a cell's neighborhood departs from flat, by one of four selectable methods -- the root of summed squared differences (Riley, DeGloria, and Elliot 1999), the mean absolute difference (Wilson et al. 2007), a slope (distance-weighted) variant, or the standard deviation of the neighborhood elevations. Higher values are more rugged. Different methods capture different notions of "ruggedness"; choose the one that matches your question.
tool.usage:
"Ruggedness" means different things to different people, and no single index captures all of them, so this tool offers four related measures of how much a cell's neighborhood departs from flat. All four use a circular moving neighborhood -- a radius you choose in cells or ground units, where a radius of 1.5 cells is the classic 3 x 3 window (the focal cell and its 8 neighbors, the four diagonals sitting about 1.41 cells away) -- and all four are, unlike the Vector Ruggedness Measure (VRM) tool, sensitive to overall slope: a smooth but steep hillside scores as rugged under any of these methods, because the elevations across it really do differ. If you want a ruggedness measure that ignores overall slope and responds only to how broken the surface is, use VRM instead; if a steep even slope should count as rugged for your purposes, one of these methods is the right choice. That trade-off -- whether a flat plain and a flat but steep slope should be treated the same or differently -- is exactly the choice these tools are meant to give you.
The four methods: Riley, DeGloria, and Elliot (1999) -- the original Terrain Ruggedness Index -- is the square root of the sum of the squared elevation differences between the focal cell and each neighbor. Its values are in the DEM's own elevation units (meters or feet, whichever the DEM uses; the output metadata records which). Riley et al.'s published ruggedness classes (level, nearly level, slightly, intermediately, moderately, highly, and extremely rugged) were calibrated to this method on a 3 x 3 neighborhood, in meters -- so compare against them only when your DEM is in meters. Available online at http://download.osgeo.org/qgis/doc/reference-docs/Terrain_Ruggedness_Index.pdf
Wilson, O'Connell, Brown, Guinan, and Grehan (2007) is the mean of the absolute differences between the focal cell and its neighbors -- a variant Wilson et al. adapted from Riley for seabed terrain, and the one GDAL computes for its TRI. Because it is an average rather than a sum, it is less sensitive to how many neighbors a cell has, so it behaves more consistently at the raster edge and next to NoData, and changes less as the neighborhood grows. Its values are also in the DEM's elevation units. https://doi.org/10.1080/01490410701295962
The slope (distance-weighted) method is a variation proposed by Jeff Jenness: before squaring and summing, each elevation difference is divided by the ground distance to that neighbor. Because the four diagonal neighbors sit about 1.41 times farther from the focal cell than the four orthogonal neighbors, the standard methods above count an elevation difference to a far corner cell the same as an equal difference to a near edge cell, even though the corner represents a gentler actual gradient. Dividing each difference by distance turns it into the slope toward that neighbor, correcting for this. (Doing so is mathematically the same as measuring the slopes to the neighboring cells directly.) The result is therefore a dimensionless rise/run -- a slope-dispersion measure -- and is not comparable to the elevation-unit values of the other methods. See Jenness, J. Topographic ruggedness [lecture], Jenness Enterprises, https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/179rA7gG0r11feha-xtizP18XytDU3I7H
The standard-deviation method is the population standard deviation of all the elevations in the neighborhood, focal cell included -- the spread of the elevations themselves rather than their differences from the center cell. It is the same quantity as ArcGIS Pro's Focal Statistics tool with the Standard Deviation statistic, and is conceptually and numerically close to the Riley method. Its values are in the DEM's elevation units. This common approach and the others are compared in the same lecture cited above.
The Riley, Wilson, and standard-deviation outputs keep the DEM's own elevation units -- a DEM in feet produces a result in feet, a DEM in meters produces meters, and the output metadata records which (the units are read from the DEM's vertical coordinate system when defined, or you choose Meters or Feet below; geographic DEMs are assumed to be in meters). The slope method is the exception: it scales elevations to meters internally so that its rise/run is a correct dimensionless ratio regardless of the DEM's units, and its output is unitless. The neighborhood is circular, with the radius set in cells or in ground units (meters, kilometers, feet, or miles); on a geographic (latitude/longitude) DEM a ground-unit radius, and the slope method's neighbor distances, are computed per row on the spheroid, so the circle stays the right size and diagonal distances stay correct at any latitude. NoData is handled by ignoring missing neighbors: a value is produced wherever the focal cell and at least one neighbor are valid, so cells at the raster edge or beside a NoData hole are computed from whatever valid neighbors they have (this differs from Riley et al.'s original, which left edge cells undefined). The output is floating point and carries statistics and a histogram so it renders without a separate Calculate Statistics step; pyramids are built with bilinear resampling. This tool reads the whole DEM into memory at once.
References: Riley, S. J., S. D. DeGloria, and R. Elliot. 1999. A terrain ruggedness index that quantifies topographic heterogeneity. Intermountain Journal of Sciences 5(1-4):23-27 (http://download.osgeo.org/qgis/doc/reference-docs/Terrain_Ruggedness_Index.pdf). Wilson, M. F. J., B. O'Connell, C. Brown, J. C. Guinan, and A. J. Grehan. 2007. Multiscale terrain analysis of multibeam bathymetry data for habitat mapping on the continental slope. Marine Geodesy 30(1-2):3-35 (https://doi.org/10.1080/01490410701295962). Jenness, J. Topographic ruggedness [lecture]. Jenness Enterprises (https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/179rA7gG0r11feha-xtizP18XytDU3I7H).

dialogReference.para: The elevation raster (DEM) to compute the ruggedness index from. It must be single band. Choose a raster from the map or browse to one on disk. Both projected and geographic (latitude/longitude) coordinate systems are supported.

The output ruggedness raster (floating point). For the Riley, Wilson, and standard-deviation methods the values are in the DEM's own elevation units (meters or feet - recorded in the output metadata); for the slope method they are a dimensionless rise/run. NoData where the focal cell is NoData or has no valid neighbor. A suggested name is filled in from the input.

Which ruggedness measure to compute. All four use the neighborhood set below; the first three respond to overall slope (a smooth steep slope scores as rugged), so pick the one whose definition of ruggedness matches your question.

Riley et al. 1999 (root of summed squared differences): the original Terrain Ruggedness Index - the square root of the summed squared differences between the focal cell and each neighbor. Output in the DEM's elevation units; Riley et al.'s published ruggedness classes were calibrated to this method on a 3 x 3 window in meters. Riley, S. J., S. D. DeGloria, and R. Elliot. 1999. Intermountain Journal of Sciences 5(1-4):23-27, http://download.osgeo.org/qgis/doc/reference-docs/Terrain_Ruggedness_Index.pdf

Wilson et al. 2007 (mean absolute difference): the mean of the absolute differences between the focal cell and its neighbors - the variant GDAL uses. Being a mean, it is more stable at edges and across neighborhood sizes. Output in the DEM's elevation units. Wilson, M. F. J., et al. 2007. Marine Geodesy 30(1-2):3-35, https://doi.org/10.1080/01490410701295962

Slope (distance-weighted, Jenness): each elevation difference is divided by the ground distance to that neighbor before squaring, so a difference to a far diagonal cell is not counted the same as an equal difference to a near edge cell. This is equivalent to measuring the slopes to the neighboring cells. The output is a dimensionless rise/run and is not comparable to the elevation-unit methods. Jenness, J. Topographic ruggedness [lecture], https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/179rA7gG0r11feha-xtizP18XytDU3I7H

Standard deviation of neighborhood elevations: the population standard deviation of every elevation in the neighborhood, focal cell included - the same quantity as Focal Statistics (Standard Deviation). Output in the DEM's elevation units. A common approach, discussed in the lecture cited above.

How far the circular neighborhood extends around each cell, in the radius units below. The default, 1.5 cells, reproduces the classic 3 x 3 window (the focal cell and its 8 immediate neighbors, as in Riley et al. 1999; the four diagonal cells sit about 1.41 cells away, so 1.5 includes them). A radius of exactly 1 cell gives a smaller 4-neighbor "plus". Larger radii measure ruggedness at a coarser scale and generally give larger values; Riley et al.'s published classes apply only to the 3 x 3 case.

The units of the radius. Cells applies the same radius everywhere, in cell widths. Meters, Kilometers, Feet, and Miles set a true ground radius, converted to cells from the raster's cell size - planarly for projected rasters, and per row on the spheroid (geodesic) for geographic rasters, so the neighborhood stays the right size at any latitude.

The DEM's elevation units, Meters or Feet. Filled in and locked automatically when the DEM defines a vertical coordinate system; geographic DEMs are assumed to be in meters. You are only asked to choose when the DEM does not say. These are the units of the output for the Riley, Wilson, and standard-deviation methods (the values are left in the DEM's own units - a feet DEM yields a feet result), and they are recorded in the output metadata. The slope method scales elevations to meters internally, so this setting does not change its unitless rise/run output.

scriptExample.title: TRI example (stand-alone script)
scriptExample.para: The classic Riley 3x3 index, then the slope (distance-weighted) variant for comparison.
scriptExample.code: import arcpy arcpy.ImportToolbox(r"C:\path\to\JennessEnterprisesTools.pyt") # your installed path is shown in this tool's run messages arcpy.jenness.TRI( in_raster=r"C:\Project\Elev.gdb\DEM", out_raster=r"C:\Project\Elev.gdb\DEM_TRI_Riley", method="Riley et al. 1999 (root of summed squared differences)", radius=1.5, radius_units="Cells", elev_units="Meters") arcpy.jenness.TRI( in_raster=r"C:\Project\Elev.gdb\DEM", out_raster=r"C:\Project\Elev.gdb\DEM_TRI_Slope", method="Slope (distance-weighted, Jenness)", radius=1.5, radius_units="Cells", elev_units="Meters")

dataIdInfo.idPurp: Terrain Ruggedness Index: a per-cell neighborhood measure of how much the surface departs from flat, with four selectable methods (Riley et al. 1999; Wilson et al. 2007; a slope/distance-weighted variant; or neighborhood standard deviation).
dataIdInfo.idAbs: Computes a Terrain Ruggedness Index from a single-band DEM over a square moving neighborhood (radius in cells; radius 1 is the classic 3 x 3 window). Four methods are offered: Riley, DeGloria, and Elliot (1999), the root of the summed squared differences between the focal cell and its neighbors; Wilson et al. (2007), the mean absolute difference (the GDAL variant); a slope (distance-weighted) variant that divides each difference by the distance to that neighbor, yielding a dimensionless slope-dispersion measure that corrects for diagonal neighbors being farther away; and the population standard deviation of the neighborhood elevations. The first three respond to overall slope; for a slope-independent measure use the Vector Ruggedness Measure (VRM) tool instead. The Riley, Wilson, and standard-deviation outputs keep the DEM's own elevation units (feet or meters, recorded in the metadata); the slope method scales to meters internally and outputs a unitless rise/run. The neighborhood is circular, radius in cells or ground units (geodesic per row on geographic DEMs). NoData is handled by ignoring missing neighbors. The output carries statistics and a histogram. References: Riley, S. J., S. D. DeGloria, and R. Elliot. 1999. Intermountain Journal of Sciences 5(1-4):23-27; Wilson, M. F. J., et al. 2007. Marine Geodesy 30(1-2):3-35.
